title: Weekly silence
hookLine: a longer sit, thirty minutes or more; Elijah on Horeb heard the still small voice only after the wind, the earthquake and the fire
tomorrow: one day of creation never gets called good. which one, and why?

cards: Thirty minutes of silence sounds restful until about minute four, when the mind starts its own playlist. Elijah's long silence came after a disaster. He has just faced down a king, and now the queen wants him dead.
He runs into the desert, sits under a juniper tree, and asks to die. An angel wakes him, twice, with bread and water. Then he walks to Horeb, the mountain of God, and lodges in a cave.
A voice asks him: What doest thou here, Elijah?

teach.b: He's told to stand on the mountain, because the LORD is passing by. Then comes the noise.

teach.h: THE LORD WAS NOT IN THE WIND.
teach.b: A great wind tears at the mountains and breaks the rocks, "but the LORD was not in the wind." Then an earthquake, and the LORD is not in the earthquake. Then a fire, and not in the fire.

teach.h: AFTER THE FIRE, A STILL SMALL VOICE.
teach.b: "And after the fire a still small voice." Elijah wraps his face in his mantle and steps out to the mouth of the cave. And the voice asks him the same question it asked in the dark: what are you doing here?
This time he hears it standing up, at the mouth of the cave.

teach.h: FIRST THE NOISE, THEN THE QUIET.
teach.b: In this story from the Hebrew Bible, God meets Elijah not in the spectacle but in the quiet left when the spectacle has passed. The King James Bible's words for that quiet are a still small voice. Notice the order, too.
First Elijah eats and sleeps. Then the wind, the earthquake, the fire. Only then, the voice.
Nobody in the story hurries it.

That's why a weekly silence is longer than a daily one. The first stretch of a long sit can be wind and fire: the list, the replayed argument, the itch. The quiet tends to come after, if you're still there.
Thirty minutes isn't a test of strength. It's simply long enough for the fire to burn down.

how: People who keep a weekly silence often set a fixed half hour or longer on the same day each week, in a quiet room, a chapel or outdoors; Quaker meetings for worship gather in shared silence.

o: one longer sit a week, past the first noise
a vow to speak to no one for a whole week
a weekly hour of quiet music or chanting

games.q: Elijah at Horeb: tap the pairs.
p: woke him with bread and water
the LORD was not in them

s: God spoke to Elijah in the earthquake
the text says the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. the voice came after.
before Horeb, an angel woke Elijah twice to eat
he was woken twice with bread and water, and slept between. rest came before the silence.
in the story, the quiet comes first and the noise after
it's the other way around: wind, earthquake and fire, then the still small voice.

games.q: minute twelve of a thirty-minute sit, and your mind is still a storm: lists, a replayed fight. what fits Elijah's story?
o: stay: the still small voice came only after the wind, the quake and the fire.
stop: if the quiet isn't there in the first minutes, it isn't coming.
switch to music, since the still small voice was really a kind of song.
games.why: on Horeb the noise came first and the LORD was not in it. the still small voice came after the fire, to someone who was still there.

practice: Open your calendar and choose one stretch this week, thirty minutes or more, for a longer sit, and name it like an appointment. Then, for these two minutes, sit still and let whatever wind comes, come. Don't chase it off.

wordCard.voice: Weekly silence: one longer sit each week, long enough for the wind and the fire to pass, and for whatever comes after them.

orig.note: Hebrew, 1 Kings 19:12: the words the KJV renders a still small voice. Some readers hear a sound of thin silence.
